weeks.title: Work with real data
weeks.subtitle: Paths, JSON, CSV, and clean records

weeks.title: Prove it to yourself
weeks.subtitle: Independent builds and a next step

lessons.title: Your first small win
lessons.concept: A variable names a value. A function takes inputs and returns a result. return sends a value back; print only displays it. Python uses indentation to group the body of a function.
lessons.task: Write add_xp(current, earned). Return the total XP after earning more. Do not print the result.
lessons.name: add_xp
lessons.solution:
def add_xp(current, earned):
    return current + earned
hints: Which arithmetic operation combines two amounts?
Use both inputs in an addition, then return the result.
lessons.extension: Add a bonus input with a default of 0, and try calling the function with two and three arguments.

lessons.title: Turn numbers into decisions
lessons.concept: Comparisons produce True or False. An if branch runs only when its condition is true. Use >= when the boundary value should count.
lessons.task: Write can_buy(coins, price). Return True if the player can afford the item, including when the amounts are equal.
lessons.name: can_buy
lessons.solution:
def can_buy(coins, price):
    return coins >= price
hints: Consider the equal case before choosing a comparison.
coins needs to be greater than or equal to price.
lessons.extension: Return the coins remaining after purchase in a separate function. Decide how to represent an unaffordable purchase.

lessons.title: Rules with boundaries
lessons.concept: Use if, elif, and else for mutually exclusive outcomes. Put more specific conditions before general ones. A return exits the function immediately.
lessons.task: Write health_label(hp): return "down" for hp <= 0, "low" for 1–25, and "ready" for anything above 25.
lessons.name: health_label
hints: Test 0, 25, and 26 on paper.
Handle hp <= 0 first, then hp <= 25, then return the final label.
lessons.extension: Add a "critical" category for 1–10 and write your own boundary examples.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: reward calculator
lessons.concept: A checkpoint combines skills without a worked example. First write the inputs, outputs, and two examples in your notes. Implement one rule at a time.
lessons.task: Write reward(score, won). Start with score * 2 XP. Add 50 if won is True. Return the total.
lessons.name: reward
hints: Calculate base XP first.
Store score * 2 in total, add 50 conditionally, then return total.
lessons.extension: Rebuild from a blank editor tomorrow without notes. Add a streak bonus only after the original works.

lessons.title: Repeat without repeating yourself
lessons.concept: A for loop visits each item. An accumulator starts with an identity value, then changes on every iteration. For a sum, start at 0.
lessons.task: Write total_damage(hits), returning the sum of all numbers in hits. Use a loop for this exercise. Empty input should return 0.
lessons.name: total_damage
hints: You need one variable that survives each iteration.
Initialize total before the loop. Add each hit inside it. Return after the loop.
lessons.extension: Implement the same behavior with sum(), then explain the loop version without looking.

lessons.title: Find what matters
lessons.concept: A filter keeps only items matching a condition. Build a new list with append instead of changing the list you are traversing.
lessons.task: Write affordable(prices, budget). Return a new list of prices <= budget, preserving the original order.
lessons.name: affordable
hints: Use the can-buy comparison inside a loop.
Start result = [], append when price <= budget, return result.
lessons.extension: Return item names instead when input contains pairs of name and price.

lessons.title: Clean a player name
lessons.concept: Strings are immutable: methods return new strings. strip() removes outer whitespace; lower() changes letter case. Chain transformations when the sequence is clear.
lessons.task: Write normalize_name(name). Strip outer whitespace, convert to lowercase, and replace each space with an underscore.
lessons.name: normalize_name
lessons.solution:
def normalize_name(name):
    return name.strip().lower().replace(" ", "_")
hints: Apply the transformations in the order requested.
Use strip(), lower(), and replace(" ", "_").
lessons.extension: Try split() and "_".join(...) to collapse repeated spaces. Explain how this changes the contract.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: score summary
lessons.concept: Decompose a problem into a loop, a condition, and a returned result. A threshold usually includes a boundary: read the >= or > requirement carefully.
lessons.task: Write count_wins(scores, target). Count how many scores are >= target. Return an integer, not a list.
lessons.name: count_wins
hints: Count matches, rather than adding their values.
Use an accumulator initialized to 0 and increment only on a match.
lessons.extension: Return both qualifying scores and their count in a dictionary.

lessons.title: Keep an inventory
lessons.concept: Dictionaries map unique keys to values. get(key, default) avoids a KeyError for missing items. copy() makes a separate top-level dictionary.
lessons.task: Write add_item(inventory, item). Return a copy of inventory with item count increased by 1. Missing items start at 0. Leave the original unchanged.
lessons.name: add_item
lessons.solution:
def add_item(inventory, item):
    result = inventory.copy()
    result[item] = result.get(item, 0) + 1
    return result
hints: Copy the dictionary before changing a count.
Use result.get(item, 0) + 1 as the new value.
lessons.extension: Write remove_item with a clear rule for missing or zero-count items.

lessons.title: A leaderboard that makes sense
lessons.concept: sorted() creates a new list. A key function chooses the comparison value. reverse=True puts larger values first; Python sorting preserves ties in input order.
lessons.task: Write leaderboard(players). Input is a list of dictionaries with name and score. Return player names sorted by score descending. Preserve input order for ties.
lessons.name: leaderboard
hints: Sort the records, then extract names.
Use key=lambda p: p["score"] and reverse=True.
lessons.extension: Change the tie rule to alphabetical name ordering and test it.

lessons.title: Remove duplicate collectibles
lessons.concept: A set records membership. To preserve first-seen order, use a set for checking and a list for the result. A plain set does not promise your desired output order.
lessons.example:
seen = set()
seen.add("star")
print("star" in seen)
lessons.task: Write unique_items(items). Return each string once, in its first-seen order.
lessons.name: unique_items
hints: You need both fast membership checking and ordered output.
When an item is not in seen, add it to both collections.
lessons.extension: Make a case-insensitive version while preserving the first spelling.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: loot report
lessons.concept: A frequency table is a dictionary whose values count occurrences. Each iteration updates one key. Think about the empty dictionary before the first item arrives.
lessons.example: No new syntax. Combine a loop with dictionary get().
lessons.task: Write loot_counts(items), returning a dictionary mapping each item string to its number of occurrences.
lessons.name: loot_counts
hints: Each item selects the key to update.
Use counts[item] = counts.get(item, 0) + 1.
lessons.extension: Use the counts to find the most common drop. Specify how ties should work.

lessons.title: Model a turn
lessons.concept: Game state is just data. Make a function for one state transition, then reuse it. max(a, b) is useful when a result must never fall below a boundary.
lessons.task: Write take_hit(hp, damage, armor). Effective damage is max(0, damage - armor). Return remaining hp, clamped at 0. Assume all inputs are nonnegative.
lessons.name: take_hit
hints: Clamp damage, then clamp health.
Compute effective damage before subtracting it from hp.
lessons.extension: Separate the damage calculation into its own function and test both functions.

lessons.title: A grid is a coordinate system
lessons.concept: Represent a 2D position as x and y. A dictionary can translate commands into movement vectors. get() can define behavior for unknown commands.
lessons.example:
dx, dy = (1, 0)
x, y = 3 + dx, 2 + dy
lessons.task: Write move(x, y, command). N adds 1 to y; S subtracts 1; E adds 1 to x; W subtracts 1. Unknown commands leave position unchanged. Return a list [x, y].
lessons.name: move
hints: Only one coordinate changes for each valid command.
Use a mapping from command to (dx, dy), defaulting to (0, 0).
lessons.extension: Add bounds for a 5×5 map. Decide whether invalid movement clamps or stays put.

lessons.title: Simulate a battle
lessons.concept: A while loop repeats while its condition is true. Ensure something changes toward termination. Define what happens for invalid input to prevent an infinite loop.
lessons.task: Write turns_to_defeat(hp, damage). Return the number of attacks needed to reduce hp to 0. Return 0 for hp <= 0 and -1 when hp > 0 but damage <= 0.
lessons.name: turns_to_defeat
hints: Handle impossible fights before entering the loop.
Subtract damage each turn and count iterations until hp <= 0.
lessons.extension: Find an arithmetic solution. Explain when it might outperform repeated subtraction.

lessons.title: Build: a tiny dungeon engine
lessons.concept: A small project can have one reliable core before it has graphics or menus. State transitions are easier to test when they do not depend on keyboard input.
lessons.example: Your engine consumes a list of commands.
lessons.task: Write dungeon(commands). Start at [0, 0]. Apply N/S/E/W movement as before. Ignore unknown commands. Return the final [x, y].
lessons.name: dungeon
hints: Reuse the idea from the movement exercise.
Keep x and y outside the loop; update for each command.
lessons.extension: Download the code. In VS Code add a printed map, walls, a treasure square, and a replay loop. Keep the engine testable.

lessons.title: Make invalid input ordinary
lessons.concept: int() converts a numeric string but raises ValueError on invalid text. Catch the specific exception you expect. Do not hide unrelated programming errors with a broad except.
lessons.task: Write parse_level(text). Return int(text) when it is an integer from 1 through 100; otherwise return None. Input is always a string.
lessons.name: parse_level
hints: Conversion can fail before you check the range.
Wrap only conversion in try/except ValueError, then check 1 <= value <= 100.
lessons.extension: Write five invalid examples of your own and state why each should fail.

lessons.title: Debug the smallest failing example
lessons.concept: Debug with a reproducible input, an expected result, and the actual result. Off-by-one errors appear at boundaries. Read the loop condition rather than guessing.
lessons.example:
Buggy idea: for i in range(1, n)
This excludes n.
lessons.task: Write sum_to(n), returning 1 + 2 + ... + n for a nonnegative integer n. The previous version forgot to include n.
lessons.name: sum_to
lessons.solution:
def sum_to(n):
    return sum(range(1, n + 1))
hints: range stops before its second argument.
Use range(1, n + 1), or use n * (n + 1) // 2.
lessons.extension: Put the buggy version in the editor first and observe which tests catch the bug. Record the root cause in your notes.

lessons.title: Validate before you calculate
lessons.concept: Validation should make assumptions explicit. any() tests whether at least one item satisfies a condition. Return early when the input violates a rule.
lessons.task: Write average_score(scores). Return None for an empty list or if any number is negative. Otherwise return the arithmetic mean. Inputs are numbers.
lessons.name: average_score
hints: Check empty input before dividing by len(scores).
Use two guards: no scores, or at least one negative score.
lessons.extension: Change the contract to raise ValueError instead. Compare how callers must handle the two designs.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: resilient settings
lessons.concept: A robust parser translates a small vocabulary and rejects the rest. A dictionary can express a set of exact accepted values more clearly than many branches.
lessons.example: Sketch accepted inputs and a fallback.
lessons.task: Write parse_bool(text). After stripping whitespace and lowercasing, return True for "yes", "true", "1"; False for "no", "false", "0"; otherwise None.
lessons.name: parse_bool
hints: Normalize once, then look up the result.
A dictionary get() returns None for an unknown key by default.
lessons.extension: Build a settings dictionary using this parser and your integer parser. Report which fields were invalid.

lessons.title: Read structured data
lessons.concept: JSON represents lists, dictionaries, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. json.loads parses text; json.dumps serializes data. JSON strings require double quotes.
lessons.task: Write load_scores(text). Parse a JSON list of numbers and return its sum. All supplied JSON is valid and contains a list of numbers.
lessons.name: load_scores
hints: Use the standard library rather than splitting the text.
json.loads(text) gives you a normal Python list.
lessons.extension: Handle invalid JSON and valid JSON with the wrong shape. Avoid catching unrelated errors.

lessons.title: CSV without the split trap
lessons.concept: CSV fields can contain commas inside quotes. csv.DictReader handles this correctly and yields a dictionary for each row. io.StringIO treats text like a readable file.
lessons.task: Write csv_total(text). CSV has headers item,price. Return the sum of prices as a float. Prices are valid numbers; fields may contain quoted commas.
lessons.name: csv_total
hints: The csv module handles quoted fields.
Pass io.StringIO(text) into csv.DictReader, then convert each price with float().
lessons.extension: Export a CSV report with csv.DictWriter. Try a title containing a comma and a quotation mark.

lessons.title: Paths are data too
lessons.concept: pathlib gives paths meaningful operations. PurePosixPath is useful for platform-independent exercises. suffix extracts an extension; name extracts the final component.
lessons.task: Write extension_counts(paths). Count lowercase file extensions including the dot; ignore paths without an extension. Treat these as POSIX-style file paths.
lessons.name: extension_counts
hints: Normalize the extension before counting.
Use PurePosixPath(path).suffix.lower() as the dictionary key.
lessons.extension: In VS Code use Path.iterdir() on a test folder you create. Print a report without changing any files.

lessons.title: Build: a playtime report
lessons.concept: A useful tool starts by separating transformation from file access. This lets you check calculations using small in-memory examples before touching real data.
lessons.task: Write playtime_report(records). Each record has game and minutes. Sum minutes per game. Return a dictionary of totals.
lessons.name: playtime_report
hints: A game title is the key of your accumulator.
For each record, add its minutes to totals.get(game, 0).
lessons.extension: Download the function. Read records from a JSON file, sort the report, and write totals to CSV in VS Code.

lessons.title: A dry run before action
lessons.concept: Automation is safer when planning and execution are separate. A planner returns intended changes as data, which you can inspect before files are renamed.
lessons.example: A rename plan is a list of [old_name, new_name] pairs.
lessons.task: Write rename_plan(names). Replace spaces with underscores and lowercase each name. Return [old, new] pairs only for names that would change.
lessons.name: rename_plan
hints: Transform each name, then compare old and new.
Append a two-element list only when new != name.
lessons.extension: Detect collisions before applying any rename. For example, "A.txt" and "a.txt" target the same name.

lessons.title: Notice a collision
lessons.concept: A plan that maps multiple sources to the same destination is ambiguous. A set tracks destinations already observed; another set can record conflicts.
lessons.task: Write duplicate_targets(plan). Each pair is [source, target]. Return sorted unique target names that appear more than once.
lessons.name: duplicate_targets
hints: The same duplicate should appear only once in your answer.
Check seen first, add collisions to a set, then sort that set.
lessons.extension: Also check targets against unchanged existing files before implementing a real rename tool.

lessons.title: Make reruns predictable
lessons.concept: An idempotent transformation gives the same result when repeated. Small pure functions make automation easier to retry, test, and inspect.
lessons.task: Write clean_tags(tags). Strip and lowercase each tag, remove empty tags, deduplicate, and return alphabetical order.
lessons.name: clean_tags
lessons.solution:
def clean_tags(tags):
    return sorted({tag.strip().lower() for tag in tags if tag.strip()})
hints: Normalize before deduplicating.
A set comprehension can normalize and filter; sorted() creates the output list.
lessons.extension: Verify clean_tags(clean_tags(tags)) == clean_tags(tags) on five examples.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: automation audit
lessons.concept: An audit summarizes what will happen without changing anything. Keep calculations separate from the eventual execution layer. Every summary field should have a clear definition.
lessons.example: Plan first. Inspect second. Execute later.
lessons.task: Write audit(plan). Return {"changes": number of pairs, "conflicts": number of distinct repeated target names}. Each pair is [source, target].
lessons.name: audit
hints: Count target frequencies, then count how many frequencies exceed 1.
Use len(plan) for changes; duplicate groups count once each.
lessons.extension: Combine rename_plan, duplicate_targets, and audit into a read-only command-line preview in VS Code.

lessons.title: Search with a clear contract
lessons.concept: Linear search scans from left to right, taking O(n) time in the worst case. enumerate gives both an index and a value. Return immediately at the first match.
lessons.task: Write first_index(values, target). Return the first matching index, or -1 if absent. Implement the search with a loop.
lessons.name: first_index
hints: The absent result belongs after the entire loop.
Use enumerate, test equality, and return the index.
lessons.extension: Explain best and worst case work. What input makes the function inspect every item?

lessons.title: Trade space for speed
lessons.concept: A set can replace repeated scans. Membership is average O(1), so checking duplicates this way is average O(n) time with O(n) extra space.
lessons.example:
if value in seen:
    return True
lessons.task: Write has_duplicate(values), returning True if any number repeats, otherwise False.
lessons.name: has_duplicate
hints: Remember what you have seen, rather than comparing every pair.
Check membership before adding each value to seen.
lessons.extension: Write the nested-loop version and explain why doubling n can multiply its comparisons by roughly four.

lessons.title: Your first hash-map problem
lessons.concept: For two-sum, remember the indices of earlier values. At each number x, ask whether target - x was already seen. Checking before storing prevents reusing the same index.
lessons.task: Write two_sum(nums, target). Return indices [earlier, current] for the first pair found while scanning left to right. Return [] if absent. Preserve the first index stored for a value.
lessons.name: two_sum
hints: Store number → index in a dictionary.
Look for target - value before storing value. Keep its first occurrence.
lessons.extension: Explain the approach aloud in 60 seconds, including duplicate values and time/space complexity.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: anagram checker
lessons.concept: Anagrams have the same character counts, not just the same unique characters. A frequency table records multiplicity. Define normalization before comparing text.
lessons.example: "aab" and "abb" contain the same set but are not anagrams.
lessons.task: Write is_anagram(a, b). Ignore spaces and letter case, but preserve all other characters. Return whether character counts match.
lessons.name: is_anagram
hints: A set loses the number of occurrences.
Build counts for each normalized string, then compare dictionaries.
lessons.extension: Implement with collections.Counter, then compare it with your own frequency table.

lessons.title: Two pointers, one invariant
lessons.concept: Two pointers can compare opposite ends of a sequence. At each step the already-inspected outer pairs match. Stop when the pointers meet or cross.
lessons.task: Write is_palindrome(text). Compare the string exactly as supplied, case-sensitive and including spaces. Return True for an empty string. Use two pointers.
lessons.name: is_palindrome
hints: Compare text[left] with text[right].
On a match, move left forward and right backward; on a mismatch return False.
lessons.extension: Create a normalized variant that ignores punctuation and case, without changing the original function contract.

lessons.title: A stack remembers unfinished work
lessons.concept: A stack is last-in, first-out. append pushes; pop removes the last value. Parentheses are balanced when every closing symbol has an unmatched opening symbol and none remain at the end.
lessons.task: Write balanced(text). Check only ( and ); ignore all other characters. Return whether parentheses are balanced.
lessons.name: balanced
hints: An unmatched closing parenthesis fails immediately.
Check the stack before popping. At the end it must be empty.
lessons.extension: Extend to (), [], and {}. Use a dictionary from closing symbols to their required opening symbols.

lessons.title: Slide a window
lessons.concept: For fixed-size contiguous windows, keep a running sum. Advancing one position subtracts the outgoing value and adds the incoming value. This avoids resumming every window.
lessons.task: Write max_window_sum(nums, k). Return the largest sum of any contiguous k values. Return None if k <= 0 or k > len(nums).
lessons.name: max_window_sum
hints: Initialize best using the first window, not 0, because numbers may be negative.
Slide by removing nums[right-k] and adding nums[right].
lessons.extension: Compare the number of additions with the brute-force approach. Try a variable-length window problem next.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: binary search
lessons.concept: Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted search interval. Its worst-case work is O(log n). The interval boundaries must move past mid to ensure termination.
lessons.task: Write binary_search(nums, target). nums is sorted ascending with unique values. Return the matching index or -1. Use binary search.
lessons.name: binary_search
hints: Draw the remaining inclusive interval after each comparison.
Use left <= right, then move a boundary to mid + 1 or mid - 1.
lessons.extension: Trace a missing target by hand. Explain why sorting an unsorted list first changes total cost.

lessons.title: Give state a home
lessons.concept: A class groups state and behavior. __init__ initializes an instance; self refers to that instance. Instance methods should preserve the rules you set for valid state.
lessons.task: Write counter_value(start, increments). Define a small Counter class inside the function with value and add(amount), then apply each increment and return the final value.
lessons.name: counter_value
hints: The class stores a value; the method changes it.
Instantiate Counter(start), call add for each amount, then return counter.value.
lessons.extension: Move the class to module scope in VS Code. Add tests with two independent instances. The numeric checks here verify behavior; inspect your class structure yourself.

lessons.title: Keep responsibilities small
lessons.concept: Decomposition makes a pipeline readable. Each helper should do one transformation, with names that describe the result. Avoid hiding unrelated actions in one function.
lessons.task: Write search_games(games, query). Each game is a string. Return matching titles in alphabetical order, using case-insensitive substring matching with outer query whitespace stripped.
lessons.name: search_games
hints: Normalize the query once, but preserve original game titles.
Use needle in game.lower(), then sort the original strings.
lessons.extension: Separate matching into a helper and add a CLI that accepts a query from the user.

lessons.title: Protect an invariant
lessons.concept: An invariant is a rule that should stay true through every operation. For a wallet, one useful rule is that balance never becomes negative. Invalid actions should leave it unchanged.
lessons.example: Before and after every transaction: balance >= 0.
lessons.task: Write wallet(balance, transactions). Nonnegative numbers deposit funds. Negative numbers withdraw only if sufficient funds exist. Ignore unaffordable withdrawals. Return the final balance. Initial balance is nonnegative.
lessons.name: wallet
hints: Check the proposed new balance before accepting an action.
Apply a transaction only if balance + amount >= 0.
lessons.extension: Return an audit trail with accepted/rejected flags and balance after each transaction.

lessons.title: Build: a reliable score service
lessons.concept: A service can be a set of pure functions before it becomes a web API. Choose a clear policy for repeated updates, missing players, and ranking ties.
lessons.example: Records → best score per player → ranked names
lessons.task: Write best_players(records). Each record has name and score. Keep each player’s highest score, then return names ordered by descending best score with alphabetical ties.
lessons.name: best_players
hints: Do not default a missing player to 0: valid scores can be negative.
Build best first, then sort names with key (-best[name], name).
lessons.extension: In VS Code persist scores to JSON and write a README with input examples, tie policy, and how to run tests.

lessons.title: Write a specification you can test
lessons.concept: A spec defines valid input and exact output before implementation. For messy data, normalize one record at a time. Preserve meaning while removing accidental differences.
lessons.task: Write normalize_game(record). Return {"title": stripped title, "minutes": int(minutes), "tags": sorted unique lowercase stripped nonempty tags}. All required keys and convertible minutes exist.
lessons.name: normalize_game
lessons.solution:
def normalize_game(record):
    return {"title": record["title"].strip(), "minutes": int(record["minutes"]), "tags": sorted({tag.strip().lower() for tag in record["tags"] if tag.strip()})}
hints: Solve each output field separately before combining them.
Reuse your clean_tags approach for tags and int() for minutes.
lessons.extension: Write a one-page spec for a game-library organizer: commands, file format, error cases, and examples.

lessons.title: Merge without losing information
lessons.concept: When duplicate records arrive, define a merge policy for each field. Group by a normalized key but preserve a useful display value. Independent fields may need different operations.
lessons.example: Same title ignoring case → combine minutes
lessons.task: Write merge_library(records). Records have title and minutes. Strip and lowercase titles for keys, sum minutes, and return a dictionary of title → total minutes.
lessons.name: merge_library
hints: The normalized title is your grouping key.
Normalize each title before looking up its current total.
lessons.extension: Merge tags too, preserving a human-readable title and documenting which spelling wins.

lessons.title: Export something useful
lessons.concept: Serialization formats need to round-trip reliably. csv.writer quotes special fields automatically. A consistent sort order makes exported files easy to inspect and compare.
lessons.example: Use io.StringIO(newline="") as a text output buffer.
lessons.task:
Write export_library(library). library is title → minutes. Return CSV text with title,minutes header, titles sorted alphabetically, and 
 line endings. Use csv.writer.
lessons.name: export_library
hints: Do not assemble CSV fields with commas yourself.
Use writer.writerow for the header and each sorted item, then output.getvalue().
lessons.extension: Save the exported text to a file in VS Code. Open it in a spreadsheet and check the quoted-title case.

lessons.title: Ship: game-library organizer
lessons.concept: Shipping includes explaining how another person can run the tool. Your core logic should remain usable without a CLI, so tests can call it directly.
lessons.task: Write library_summary(records). Return {"games": number of distinct stripped lowercase titles, "minutes": sum of all minutes}. Each record has title and numeric minutes.
lessons.name: library_summary
hints: Unique normalized titles determine games; all records contribute minutes.
Use a set for titles and sum for minutes.
lessons.extension: Ship in VS Code: combine weeks 6–11 into a CLI with import, search, report, and export commands. Include sample data, tests, and a README. Browser checks validate only the core summary here.

lessons.title: Independent build: tournament table
lessons.concept: Start with a blank function body. Write a plan in ordinary language, then create your own examples. Hints remain available, but a completion using them counts as guided practice.
lessons.example: Spend 5 minutes planning before writing Python.
lessons.task: Write tournament(matches). Each match is [winner, loser]. A win awards 3 points; a loss awards 0. Include all players. Return [name, points] pairs sorted by points descending and name ascending.
lessons.name: tournament
hints: Initialize losing players too, even if they never win.
Count points in a dictionary, sort names by (-points[name], name), then build pairs.
lessons.extension: Add draws, invalid self-matches, and a CSV importer. Write the rules before changing the implementation.

lessons.title: Independent build: log analyzer
lessons.concept: Logs are data with a grammar. Decide how to handle malformed records explicitly. Keep parsing and counting separable so a bad line does not corrupt your summary.
lessons.task: Write log_counts(lines). Split each line at its first |. Strip and uppercase the level. Count only INFO, WARN, ERROR; ignore lines without | or with unknown levels. Return a dictionary containing only levels seen.
lessons.name: log_counts
hints: Validate the separator before extracting the level.
split("|", 1)[0] selects the level; normalize it and check membership.
lessons.extension: Apply this to a synthetic device log. Add error-rate and longest-run summaries without using real personal data.

lessons.title: Independent build: interview explanation
lessons.concept: An interview solution includes a correct algorithm, examples, and a clear complexity explanation. Solve for correctness first, then improve unnecessary work.
lessons.example: Explain why the chosen data structure fits the operation.
lessons.task: Write first_unique(text). Return the first character that occurs exactly once, preserving case and including spaces. Return None if no such character exists. Aim for O(n) time.
lessons.name: first_unique
hints: You need full counts before knowing which early character is unique.
Use two passes: count all characters, then scan the original text for count == 1.
lessons.extension: Record a two-minute explanation: approach, example, empty case, O(n) time, O(k) space for k distinct characters.

lessons.title: Final checkpoint: build from a spec
lessons.concept: Confidence is evidence accumulated across different tasks. Passing these checks is a milestone; shipping an independent project and debugging new failures are the next proof.
lessons.example: Write a plan. Implement. Test. Explain. Extend.
lessons.task: Write recommend(games, budget). Each game has title, price, rating. Keep games priced <= budget. Return up to 3 titles ranked by rating descending, then price ascending, then title alphabetically. Do not change the input list.
lessons.name: recommend
lessons.solution:
def recommend(games, budget):
    eligible = [game for game in games if game["price"] <= budget]
    ordered = sorted(eligible, key=lambda game: (-game["rating"], game["price"], game["title"]))
    return [game["title"] for game in ordered[:3]]
hints: Filter, sort with a three-part key, then take three.
The sorting key is (-rating, price, title). Use sorted() to avoid mutating the input.
